evidence.evidence_gap: The mapped numerical leaf supports pressure-force demand; the retrieval wording is original and follows the declared previous-lesson handoff.

hints: Compare the depths of the horizontal top and bottom faces.
Turn the pressure difference into a comparison of the vertical pressure forces, then account for the side faces.
walkthrough: The bottom face is deeper than the top face, so the liquid pressure is greater at the bottom.
For equal top and bottom areas, the upward pressure force on the bottom is greater than the downward pressure force on the top.
Appropriate horizontal pressure forces on opposite side faces cancel.
The remaining resultant pressure force is therefore upward.

ai_rubric.observable: States that pressure, and hence pressure force for equal face area, is greater on the deeper bottom face than on the top face.
Explains that the unequal vertical pressure forces give an upward resultant, with appropriate sideways forces cancelling.

hints: In F = ρgV, identify whether any factor changes when the same rigid object moves deeper.
Greater absolute pressure does not necessarily mean a greater difference between top and bottom pressure forces.
walkthrough: The liquid is unchanged, so ρ is constant, and g is constant.
The rigid object stays fully submerged, so it displaces the same volume V.
Therefore F = ρgV is unchanged, even though the absolute pressure is greater.
The correct option is C.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects C: the upthrust stays constant because fluid density and displaced volume stay constant.

hints: The same block has the same weight in both liquids.
For floating equilibrium, ask how V must change in ρgV = W when ρ increases.
walkthrough: The block remains at rest with no other vertical force, so its upthrust equals its unchanged weight.
The salt solution has greater density.
In F = ρgV, the same required F with greater ρ needs a smaller displaced volume V.
The correct option is B.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects B: the block displaces a smaller volume because denser fluid supports the same weight.

hints: For a uniform floating solid, equate ρ_fluid gV_submerged to ρ_object gV_total.
Cancel g and divide by the total volume to find the submerged fraction.
walkthrough: Floating equilibrium gives upthrust equal to weight.
Thus ρ_fluid gV_submerged = ρ_object gV_total.
The fraction submerged is 650/1000 = 0.65 = 65%.
The correct option is B.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects B: 65% of the solid's volume is submerged.

hints: Because the case is fully submerged, its whole external volume is the displaced-water volume.
Multiply the three dimensions, keeping every length in metres.
walkthrough: The case is fully submerged, so displaced volume equals case volume.
V = length × width × height = (0.40)(0.25)(0.18).

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates the fully displaced volume as (0.40)(0.25)(0.18) = 0.0180 m³.

hints: Use the density of the displaced water, not the density of the case.
Substitute the volume from part (a) into F = ρgV.
walkthrough: Use F = ρgV with ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ and V = 0.0180 m³.
To three significant figures, the upthrust is 177 N upward.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses F = ρgV with water density 1000 kg m⁻³ and displaced volume 0.0180 m³.
Obtains an upthrust of 177 N upward to three significant figures.

hints: Draw the case alone: weight is downward, while both upthrust and the cable pull are upward.
For zero resultant force, rearrange T + F = W.
walkthrough: The cable from above pulls the case upward.
Equilibrium gives T + 176.58 = 250.
T = 73.42 N, so the cable tension on the case is 73.4 N upward.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses vertical equilibrium as tension plus upthrust equals the 250 N weight.
Obtains a cable tension of 73.4 N acting upward on the case.

hints: The word freely excludes a cable or support force.
At rest, the vector sum of the remaining vertical forces is zero.
walkthrough: The liquid exerts upthrust upward and gravity gives weight downward.
There is no cable or support force because the float is free.
At equilibrium, the two opposite forces have equal magnitudes.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies weight downward and upthrust upward as the two vertical forces.
States that upthrust equals weight because the freely floating cylinder is in equilibrium.

hints: Set the upthrust ρgV equal to the weight mg.
Cancel g before substituting; the displaced volume is mass divided by fluid density.
walkthrough: Floating equilibrium gives ρ_oil gV = mg.
Cancel g and rearrange: V = m/ρ_oil.

ai_rubric.observable: Equates ρ_oil gV to mg for floating equilibrium and rearranges for V.
Obtains a displaced oil volume of 0.0600 m³.

hints: For a vertical cylinder with constant area, the submerged volume is Ah.
Rearrange h = V/A using the volume from part (b).
walkthrough: The submerged cylindrical volume is V = Ah.
The submerged depth is 0.300 m.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses h = V/A to obtain a submerged depth of 0.300 m in oil.

hints: The float's mass and required equilibrium upthrust are unchanged.
Repeat V = m/ρ with the water density, then divide by the same area and compare the displaced volumes.
walkthrough: In water, floating equilibrium gives V = m/ρ_water = 48/1000 = 0.0480 m³.
The submerged depth is h = 0.0480/0.20 = 0.240 m.
Water is denser than oil, so a smaller volume of it has enough weight to provide the same upthrust.
The float therefore has a smaller submerged depth in water.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates the new submerged depth as 0.240 m in water.
Explains that denser water requires a smaller displaced volume to provide the same upthrust equal to the fixed weight.

evidence.evidence_gap: The explicit pressure-difference-to-Archimedes check combines mapped demands into an original representation chain.

hints: Compare the depth, pressure and force on the bottom face with those on the top face.
Then account for the forces on opposite side faces.
walkthrough: The bottom face is deeper than the top face, so the brine pressure is greater there.
The equal face areas mean the upward bottom force is greater than the downward top force.
Appropriate forces on opposite vertical faces cancel.
The pressure forces therefore have an upward resultant.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the deeper bottom face has greater pressure and pressure force than the top face.
Explains that the unequal vertical forces give an upward resultant while appropriate sideways forces cancel.

hints: The vertical separation of the faces is the depth difference in Δp = ρgΔh.
Substitute 0.25 m, not an absolute depth below the surface.
walkthrough: Use the hydrostatic pressure difference Δp = ρgΔh.
To three significant figures, Δp = 2.94 × 10³ Pa.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses Δp = ρgΔh with brine density 1200 kg m⁻³ and vertical separation 0.25 m.
Obtains a pressure difference of 2.94 × 10³ Pa.

hints: A pressure difference acting over the common face area gives the resultant vertical force.
For the independent check, calculate the block volume as face area multiplied by face separation.
walkthrough: For the Archimedes check, the displaced volume is V = AΔh = (0.060)(0.25) = 0.0150 m³.
The independent route confirms an upthrust of 177 N to three significant figures.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses F = ΔpA and checks with F = ρgV using V = AΔh = 0.0150 m³.
Obtains an upthrust of 176.58 N, or 177 N, by both routes.

hints: The cable comes from above, so determine the direction in which it pulls the block.
Use zero resultant force with the 210 N weight and the upthrust from part (c).
walkthrough: The cable from above pulls upward, as does the 176.58 N upthrust. Weight is 210 N downward.
Equilibrium gives T + 176.58 = 210.
The cable tension on the block is 33.4 N upward.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses vertical equilibrium as tension plus upthrust equals the 210 N weight.
Obtains a cable tension of 33.4 N acting upward on the block.
